title: Addiction and recovery
hookLine: one day at a time, with help and grace
tomorrow: Peter swore he'd never fail. so what happened after he did?

lines: IN THE BIBLE, OR A SLOGAN?
EXTRA BREAD, HIDDEN IN A TENT.
cards: Is "one day at a time" in the Bible, or just a slogan? The words are a saying from recovery groups. The idea is far older.
Anyone who has tried to quit something knows the bargain: just get through this week, this month, the rest of your life. In Exodus there is a man who tries to do the rest of his life in advance.

Last night he scraped extra bread into a pot and hid it in his tent, because what if tomorrow there is nothing? Now it is dawn in the desert, and he lifts the lid on his backup plan. It is full of worms, and it stinks.

teach.b: So why would God send bread that won't keep? The bread is manna, and the rule comes with it: gather what you need for the day. Kept overnight, it spoils.
The people have to trust there will be more tomorrow, and there is. Jesus puts that same rhythm into the prayer he teaches.
In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Give us this day our supersubstantial bread." This day, not this year. A few lines later: "Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof."

So the saying sounds like it came straight out of that desert. Something to tell a friend tonight: some recovery groups meet in parish halls, folding chairs under a crucifix. And recovery isn't treated as willpower alone.
Help counts: a sponsor, a doctor, a meeting, a friend who picks up at two in the morning. Grace counts too.
Paul begged God to take away something painful he never names, and the answer he heard was: "My grace is sufficient for thee." Not a cure on the spot. Enough for today.
Recovery doesn't ask anyone to be well forever by Friday.
It asks for today, with help, then tomorrow, with help again.
And when someone slips, the desert story has a word for that too: the bread still came the next morning.

how: Catholics pray the Our Father, with its "give us this day," at every Mass and in daily prayer; some parishes open their halls to recovery groups, and priests and parish ministers walk with people in recovery through prayer and the sacraments.

o: a weak will that just needs more effort
being hooked on something, and the road back
a bad habit you fix with one decision

games.q: the desert and the daily bread — tap the pairs.
p: bread that spoiled if kept overnight
my grace is sufficient for thee
one day at a time, with help

s: "one day at a time" is a line straight out of the Bible
the words are a recovery saying; the idea is older: manna for the day, and give us this day.
in Exodus, manna kept overnight spoiled
it bred worms and stank; the people had to trust there'd be more.
in this story, a slip means the help stops coming
the bread still came the next morning.

games.q: your uncle is newly sober and says he has to stay sober for the rest of his life, starting now. it's crushing him. what does the manna story offer?
o: only today's portion: get through today, with help.
plan every week ahead so nothing catches him off guard.
pray once for healing and trust it's done for good.
games.why: manna was gathered for one day, and Jesus taught people to ask for bread this day. one day at a time, with help and grace.

practice: Bring to mind someone in recovery, or someone you hope will get there; it can be you. Say their name quietly, then three words: just for today.
If you pray, you can add the line from the Our Father for them, give us this day our daily bread, and let the rest of the sit be for their today.

wordCard.voice: Addiction and recovery. Something that takes hold of a life, and the long road back, walked a day at a time, with help and grace.

orig.note: Greek, from Matthew 6:11: the word behind "daily" or "supersubstantial" bread; its exact sense is debated.

carryVoice: Your line: one day at a time. The manna came again the next morning. See you tomorrow.
